Figure 8 presents the duty-temperature profile for the 2-tier and 1-tier PCM cases where the HTF hot temperature is 715°C. For all these cases, the average HTF temperature within the PHX is higher with the PCMs than without (i.e., the salt-only case). This increase in average HTF temperature provides the PHX a higher driving temperature difference, enabling lower PHX conductance for a calculated effectiveness. 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nrel.gov/publications. Figure 9 presents the minimum HTF-sCO temperature difference that occurs within the PHX as 2 a function of HTF hot temperature. The 3-tier case has the greatest temperature difference at 740°C at approximately 7.5°C. For the other PCM cases, the minimum temperature difference approaches 20°C (the assumed inlet and outlet approach temperature) as the HTF hot temperature decreases from 745°C to 715°C. A minimum temperature difference of less than 20°C indicates that the PHX pinch temperature occurs internal to the PHX and not at either end of the PHX. The 2-tier 50/50 PCM case has the greatest sensitivity for HTF hot temperatures below 715°C. This is a result of the less latent heat energy during the PCM 1 phase change, which causes the HTF temperature to approach the sCO temperature before the phase change of 2 PCM 2. Figure 9. PHX minimum temperature difference as a function of HTF hot temperature for each PCM salt slurry case. Figure 10 presents the HTF mass flow rate through the PHX. All PCM cases result in a reduction of HTF mass flow compared to the salt-only case (approximately 50% reduction). The 1-tier PCM case achieves the lowest required HTF mass flow rate. However, both 2-tier PCM cases result in very similar flow rates at an HTF hot temperature of 715°C. The 1-tier PCM case is more sensitive to HTF hot temperatures below 715°C because all the HTF’s latent heat occurs between 690 and 71 °C.
